In America, there’s a popular podcast called "The Telepathy Tapes." You might have heard of it. The idea is that kids with autism are able to read their parents' minds. However, this is incorrect; they do something else. In China, a mother in the countryside—a non-educated, poor woman—has an autistic son who doesn’t speak and struggles with eye contact and schooling.

One day, the mother contacts CCTV, the national broadcaster, claiming her son can read her mind. The TV crew agrees to make a documentary. They fly down to the village, film the interaction, where the boy is isolated in a room. The mother gives him a number (e.g., five) and asks him to read her mind. The boy responds that he saw the number five. This seems remarkable but isn't believable.

The documentary team spends days figuring out what happened. They bring in artificial intelligence, which reveals that it’s the pitch of the voice giving the answer. When they confront the mother, she admits using pitch to communicate with her son, explaining their scheme was to gain television coverage and donations for her autistic child's education and professional help.

This story highlights the power of human imagination when we truly love someone, as seen in a cooperative painting exercise where uncoordinated individuals can create something amazing together. Similarly, in polo games, horses read their riders' intentions through subtle cues, showcasing the depth of empathy between partners.

These stories illustrate how hidden emotional languages and shared purposes drive creativity and cooperation.
